name: The romantic cult of Napoleon
plain_explanation: Napoleon became, for Byron and many nineteenth-century Europeans, less a historical statesman than a romantic symbol: the one force strong enough to stand against dull industrialism and shopkeeping, admired by figures across the political spectrum for his sheer individual, world-shaking power.
precise_definition: The Continental romantic phenomenon, illustrated through Byron's own proclaimed wish for Napoleon's victory during the Hundred Days and his grief at Waterloo ('I'm damned sorry for it'), in which Napoleon is transfigured into a symbol of titanic individual will opposed to bourgeois commerce and pacifism, inspiring figures as different as Clausewitz, Stendhal, Heine, Fichte, and Nietzsche, and provoking sharply divided German reactions (liberal-emancipatory versus Antichrist-nationalist).
why_it_mattered: It is the direct historical bridge Russell draws between Byron's aristocratic self-assertion and the later, more systematic philosophies of will and power in Schopenhauer and Nietzsche, and onward into twentieth-century nationalist politics.
historical_origin: The Napoleonic wars and their aftermath, refracted through Byron's poetry and biography.
associated_philosopher: Lord Byron; later synthesized, per Russell, by Bismarck and embraced by Nietzsche
examples: Byron's grief at Napoleon's abdication in 1814, briefly resolved by admiring Washington instead, until the return from Elba made this unnecessary
Bismarck's 'synthesis': Napoleon as Antichrist, but 'an Antichrist to be imitated, not merely to be abhorred'
competing_positions: Heine's view of Napoleon as liberal emancipator, destroyer of serfdom and legitimacy
The view of Napoleon as Antichrist and enemy of the German nation
influence_on_later_thinkers: Directly shapes Nietzsche's own admiration of Napoleon as a great man 'defeated by petty opponents,' discussed in the following chapter.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Feeds directly into German nationalism via Bismarck's synthesis and into Nietzsche's political philosophy.
